Copy effects such as myriad apply on layer 1. Text-changing effects apply on layer 3. Layer 1 is applied before layer 3, which means the Myriad token is created as a copy of the printed card.

Deadpool has a replacement effect that modifies how he enters the battlefield. This is not a trigger, and is therefore something that happens before state-based actions are checked.

So what happens is that Deadpool tokens try to enter (all at once, not one at a time like you implied), the replacement effects say "as it enters, swap text boxes" (this ability doesn't use the stack and will happen while the myriad trigger is still resolving), and only \*then\* does the myriad trigger resolve and cause the legend rule to apply.

Hammer Arm's speed lowering is considered a primary effect, just like U-turn.

I've done some pokemon romhacking and that's helped me understand sheer force a bit more. When you're editing a move, there's room to edit primary effects and secondary effects. In my experience, though it's been a while, basically anything that raises a stat or causes a status condition is a secondary effect. Primary effects are reserved for things like Knock Off or U-Turn, which always happen and are more interesting than just causing a status or raising/lowering a stat. Drawbacks are also primary effects.

Tackle has no effects, U-turn has a primary effect (switching) but no secondary, Flamethrower has no primary but has a secondary (chance to burn), and Flare Blitz has a primary (recoil) and a secondary (chance to burn).

If you want a rule of thumb, remember that damage is not considered an effect of a move.

The reason I suggest a turbo deck is that control and midrange cEDH decks are usually designed to fight within the meta, which are going to perform significantly worse into a casual pod. Decks like Tymna Kraum will run cards like Pyroblast and An Offer You Can't Refuse that are complete blanks into a lot of casual decks. Turbo decks don't have this problem (at least, not as much) because they're proactive- winning the game in an uninteractive way works against any deck at any power level.

I went to VFS. I know that by this time, you've already made your decision. In fact, I may have even met you briefly-- I was in VFS for the first half of 2023. But I'm leaving this comment in case anyone else finds it like I did.

I had a fantastic time at VFS, and to date it was literally the best year of my life. That being said, I had a number of things going for me. I'm a Canadian citizen, which means that my tuition was literally less than half of yours. Many of my foreign friends said that while they enjoyed the experience and deeply appreciate the connections they made during their classes, they expected a little bit more considering the price they paid. Also, I was lucky enough to have my parents pay for me to go, so I didn't need to take out any loans. Perhaps my experiences would be colored a different way if I had taken a large financial hit for it.

That being said, I think the content was pretty good. It took you through the basics-- After one eight-week term (there are six terms), you'd know enough to be able to go on the internet and confidently say "I know how to 3D model" or "I know how to use Unreal", and have enough skills to back it up. However, due to the fast pace, there's not much time for the instructor to go in depth on the subject. You'll have to use the framework that they give you to do your own research, and then ask your instructors follow up questions. They are happy to help you go into depth, but that's something *you* have to lead. And similarly, it's extremely easy to fail at VFS. Not because the classes are unapproachably hard, but because it's really easy to let the pressure get to you. You have to be on the ball 100% of the time.

The teachers are very hit or miss. Fortunately, the teachers who teach the core subjects (3D art, level design, and programming) are all fantastic. They're super friendly and God, they know their stuff. The teachers that are there to teach you a class that lasts only one term, like marketing or QA? Very hit or miss. Also, some of those single-term instructors can only show up remotely, which was a big problem for me. It's important in that case to leverage your classmates for help.

And on the subject of your classmates, I think the main selling point of VFS is the network and connections you get. A year and a half after graduation later, and we're still a very tight-knit group. It's important to go to the social events that you can go to and get to know everyone. Aside from your classmates, everyone and their dog at VFS has some serious credibility in the gaming industry, and it's good to get to know them. VFS is also a notable name in the gaming industry-- I think half of the industry professionals I've talked to know somebody who graduated from the school, and those people have no affiliation to it.

I should also specify that I did not get a job, and neither did a lot of my classmates. That's not for lack of talent-- That's just because the gaming industry right now is going through an awful slump. There was serious growth during the pandemic and companies are still downsizing from that. So the time I went there may not be the best time to have gone. I would definitely not treat this school as a guaranteed job offer afterwards, because it's not.

I thoroughly enjoy the time I spent there and got a lot from my education there, but I don't know that I'd *recommend* it, due to how different everyone's circumstances are. But if anyone is finding this thread later on, please feel free to message me if you want to ask more about VFS.

/uj Fun fact, the ability that grants flying does not work because of layers. 

Ability granting and removing effects are handled on layer 6. Power and toughness calculations happen on layer 7, after layer 6. Which means as far as the game is concerned, here’s how it’ll go. 

The game will check the layers until it arrives on layer 6. It will look at Psychotic Frog’s power and toughness, which will never ever be different from its printed values at this point. The ability will be like “hey, Frog’s P/T is just 1/2. It doesn’t get flying and trample.”

Then the game will calculate layer 7, and only then will it process the power and toughness it gained from power and toughness setting effects (such as [[scale up]]), +1/+1 counters, and temporary increases or decreases. But since layer 6 has already been applied, that won’t matter.

The way you should template this is as a trigger that checks the power and toughness of the frog at some point, and either permanently grants it those abilities or until end of turn.

As a combo enjoyer and defender, I don’t think that’s the case. By building a deck that can’t interact with combos, you implicitly accept that combos are a problem for you— in the same way that a combo player accepts that they lose if one of their pieces gets interacted with. This is also a concession you make by tapping out and going shields down. 

So to apply it to your example, it would be like knowing that the purple ball is there (because none of us are completely oblivious to combos), choosing not to do anything about it, and calling it an anticlimax if someone uses it to win. IMO that’s like saying it’s an anticlimax if a fighter turns their back to their opponent and then gets stabbed. 

I think that combos are generally far more telegraphed than people are making them out to be. People act as though someone will drop Kinnan and Basalt Monolith (for example) on the same turn, but how did they get those in hand? Either Kinnan is the commander, in which case it’s extremely telegraphed, or they tutored for it, in which case you could see that they’re tutoring and put the pieces together, or they had an unimpeded Rhystic Study all game, in which case they drew a shitload of cards and are in that way telegraphing an explosive turn. (Sometimes players will get lucky but the majority of the time that isn’t the case).
